title: How do you train managers to handle harassment complaints?
description: How to train managers to handle harassment complaints: first response, confidentiality, retaliation, escalation, records, and scored role plays.
shortAnswer: Train managers to handle harassment complaints by teaching a clear first response: listen without judgment, take every report seriously, explain confidentiality honestly, act on immediate safety, escalate through the organization's process rather than investigating alone, prevent retaliation, and record what was reported and done. Teach it through realistic role plays scored against a rubric, refresh it regularly, and test whether managers apply it, because one off awareness sessions rarely change how a manager responds.
keyTakeaways: Managers are often the first person a worker tells. How they respond in that conversation shapes whether the complaint is handled well and whether others report.
Regulator guidance in several markets lists the same manager skills: recognizing harassment, responding and supporting, escalating, confidentiality, and preventing retaliation.
Managers should not run investigations unless trained and impartial. Their role is to respond, protect, escalate and record.
Practice beats presentation. Role plays and scenario assessment show whether a manager can handle the conversation.
One off training at induction is not enough. Australia's Human Rights Commission guidance says it has proven ineffective unless periodically reinforced.

sections.heading: Why do managers need specific training on harassment complaints?

blocks.text: Managers need specific training because they carry responsibilities other employees do not: receiving reports, acting on what they see, protecting the people involved and passing matters to the right process. General awareness training does not teach those skills.

Regulators say so explicitly. The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) notes that because supervisors and managers have additional responsibilities, they may benefit from additional training, and suggests including team leaders who exercise authority ([EEOC, Promising Practices for Preventing Harassment](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/promising-practices-preventing-harassment)). Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on sexual and gender-based harassment describes manager and supervisor training that provides the skills to step in when they witness harassment and to respond to and support staff, including through referral ([Safe Work Australia, December 2023](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-sexual-and-gender-based-harassment)). Japan's power harassment guideline from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) includes training for the staff who handle consultations ([MHLW guideline](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11900000/000584512.pdf); see [Japan power harassment prevention obligations](/regulations/japan-power-harassment-prevention-obligations)).

Some jurisdictions mandate supervisor training directly. California, for example, requires employers with five or more employees to provide two hours of sexual harassment prevention training to supervisory employees every two years (see [California and New York harassment training](/regulations/california-and-new-york-harassment-training)). For a cross market view, see [workplace harassment training requirements by country](/compare/workplace-harassment-training-requirements-by-country).

sections.heading: What should manager training on harassment complaints cover?

blocks.text: It should cover how to recognize harassment, how to respond in the first conversation, confidentiality and its limits, retaliation, escalation, and the manager's own accountability. The EEOC's suggested content for supervisors and managers includes how to prevent, identify, stop, report and correct harassment; realistic methods for addressing harassment they observe or that is reported to them; clear instructions on reporting up the chain; the confidentiality rules associated with complaints; an unequivocal statement that retaliation is prohibited, with examples of protected conduct; and the consequences of failing to fulfill their responsibilities.

sections.heading: What should a manager do when someone reports harassment?

blocks.text: Listen, take it seriously, deal with immediate safety, be honest about confidentiality, escalate through the process, protect against retaliation, and record. The protocol below is an original training aid; adapt the escalation route and timings to your own policy.

items: **Make space.** Move to a private place, give your full attention, and let the person tell it their way. Do not interrupt to test their account.
**Acknowledge.** Thank them for raising it and say it will be taken seriously. Avoid judging, minimizing or promising a particular outcome.

**Check immediate safety.** Ask whether they feel safe now and whether anything needs to change straight away, such as seating, shifts or reporting lines, without disadvantaging the person who reported.

**Explain confidentiality honestly.** Say who will need to know and why. Safe Work Australia's code says workers should be made aware of any mandatory reporting or disclosure obligations that may limit confidentiality and how their information will be managed.
**Explain what happens next.** Describe the process, the options, and the support available, such as an employee assistance program or a contact officer.
**Escalate.** Refer to the designated person or function within the time your policy sets, even if the person asks you to do nothing; explain why where the organization has a duty to act.
**Guard against retaliation.** Watch for and stop adverse treatment of the person who reported and of witnesses.
**Record.** Note the date, what was reported in the person's words, what you did and to whom you referred it. Store it securely.

blocks.title: What managers should not do
blocks.text: Do not investigate alone, interview the alleged harasser, or tell the team. Do not promise absolute confidentiality. Do not encourage the person to sort it out themselves or to drop it. Do not presume the alleged harasser is guilty or discipline them before the process concludes: the EEOC recommends processes that ensure alleged harassers are not prematurely presumed guilty or prematurely disciplined.

sections.heading: Should managers investigate harassment complaints themselves?

blocks.text: Usually not. Investigations need impartial, trained investigators, and a line manager is rarely impartial. Safe Work Australia's code says investigations should be fair, transparent, timely and impartial, decision makers should be appropriately trained, unbiased and accountable, and an external investigator may be needed where no impartial internal investigator is available, for example when a senior manager is involved.

The EEOC similarly recommends that employees responsible for receiving, investigating and resolving complaints be well trained, objective and neutral, have the authority and independence to act, understand confidentiality, and document every complaint from intake to resolution. If managers do serve as contact officers or investigators, give them the additional training Safe Work Australia describes for contact officers, including trauma informed communication, explaining options and legal protections, and knowing when to escalate.

Not every matter needs a formal investigation. Safe Work Australia notes that the best response to a first incident of inappropriate language may be an immediate informal discussion. Training should help managers judge proportion, while making clear that serious or repeated conduct always goes to the formal process.

sections.heading: How should manager harassment training be delivered and refreshed?

blocks.text: Deliver it live and interactive where possible, with practice, and reinforce it over time. The EEOC says harassment training may be most effective when it is championed by senior leaders, repeated and reinforced regularly, tailored to the workplace, and conducted by qualified, live, interactive trainers, or designed for active engagement where live training is not feasible.

items: Use role plays built from realistic, workplace specific scenarios, with a trained observer scoring against the rubric above.
Include scenarios involving customers, clients or patients, not only colleagues; Safe Work Australia's code and Japan's customer harassment rules both address third party conduct.

Refresh regularly and after policy changes. The Australian Human Rights Commission's positive duty guidelines say one off training at induction has proven ineffective unless periodically reinforced (see [the positive duty and training](/regulations/positive-duty-sexual-harassment-training)).
Use short follow ups between sessions: a scenario discussion at a management meeting, or a review of how recent reports were handled.

Measure application, not completion: review a sample of manager handled reports against the protocol, and track whether reports increase in teams after training. See [measuring training effectiveness](/guides/how-to-measure-training-effectiveness).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures manager obligations, such as escalation, confidentiality and retaliation, as defined concepts linked to the policy and the regulatory sources behind them, each with assessment points such as role play rubrics. That lets an organization show which obligations each manager has been assessed on. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.q: Can a manager keep a harassment complaint confidential if asked?
faqs.a: Not always. A manager can keep it to the smallest necessary group, but often cannot promise absolute confidentiality, because the organization may have a duty to act or legal reporting obligations. Safe Work Australia's code says workers should be told about obligations that may limit confidentiality and how their information will be protected.

faqs.q: What if the complaint is about the manager's own manager?
faqs.a: The manager should use an alternative route in the policy, such as HR, a contact officer, or a senior leader outside the reporting line. The EEOC recommends multiple avenues of complaint, including one for complaints about senior leaders, and Safe Work Australia notes an external investigator may be needed where a senior manager is involved.

faqs.q: How often should managers be retrained?
faqs.a: Follow any legal interval first, such as every two years for supervisors in California. Otherwise refresh at least periodically and after policy changes or incidents. The Australian Human Rights Commission's guidelines say one off training at induction has proven ineffective unless periodically reinforced, and the EEOC recommends regular repetition and reinforcement.

faqs.q: Does online training satisfy the need for manager training?
faqs.a: It can deliver knowledge, but responding to a distressed employee is a skill best built through practice. The EEOC suggests live, interactive trainers, or active engagement where live training is not feasible. California's civil rights agency does not accept text only training for its mandated courses.
